title: Energetic cost of locomotion closely aligns with the preferred uphill walk-run transition at constant vertical speed in runners
authors: Finiel L, Carron S, Margot C, Luc V, Malatesta D, Borrani F
population: 17 endurance-trained runners walking and running at a constant vertical speed of 800 m/h
findings: 17 endurance-trained runners walked and ran 6 min bouts at a constant vertical speed of 800 m/h; the average preferred transition speed (PTS) occurred at 1.76 m/s on a 7.2 degree slope (tan 7.2 degrees = 0.126, about 12.6% grade, derived).
Energy cost of transport, O2 cost and metabolic power gave optimal transition speeds that did not differ significantly from PTS.
Heart rate, ventilation and internal mechanical work gave optimal transition speeds significantly different from PTS.
External and total mechanical work, step frequency and step length showed no crossover between gaits.
The authors conclude that uphill PTS aligns more closely with energetic crossover criteria than with cardiorespiratory or mechanical-work crossovers.
limitations: 17 trained runners, 6 min treadmill bouts at one vertical speed (800 m/h); no fatigue and no ultra durations.
implications: At about 800 m/h of climbing, trained runners chose to walk on slopes steeper than about 7 degrees (about 12.6% grade); use this as the default walk/run switch at that climbing rate and let personal data move it.
Gait choice followed energetic cost, not heart rate or ventilation. Do not set the walk/run switch from heart rate alone; use a cost or power criterion where the engine has the data.

800 m/h is one tested condition and is above the 547 m/h mean uphill vertical speed observed in a 220 km mountain ultra [jeker-2020-vertical-speed-ultra], so it is not a default hiking pace for ultras.

verification.notes: Crossref: Eur J Appl Physiol, online 2026-07-30, six authors match (no volume yet). PubMed PMID 42530641 abstract supports all numbers. Recent paper, single lab; 7.2 degrees to 12.6% grade is derived (tan).
